citation: Fergus' Historical Series, Nos. 26-29, bound in one volume (Chicago: Fergus Printing Company, 1883-1888). FOUR SEPARATELY PRINTED PAMPHLETS: No. 26, William Henry Harrison, A Discourse on the Aborigines of the Ohio Valley, with the Fort Wayne Indian speeches of 1811 appended (leaves 15-206); No. 27, Hiram W. Beckwith, The Illinois and Indiana Indians (1884, leaves 207-398); No. 28, Directory of the City of Chicago for 1843, compiled by Robert Fergus (1896, leaves 399-656); No. 29, Julia Duncan Kirby, Biographical Sketch of Joseph Duncan, Fifth Governor of Illinois (1888, leaves 657-858). T-0499 read leaves 1-429, the first half by page index; T-0500 reads the second.
author: William Henry Harrison (No. 26, the discourse, 1838); Hiram W. Beckwith (No. 27 entire, 1884, and the editorial footnotes to No. 26's appendix); Robert Fergus (No. 28, compiled 1896); Julia Duncan Kirby (No. 29, 1888)
date: 1883-1888 for the four printings; No. 28 carries 1843 on its cover and 1896 on its title page and in its signed preface
describes_date: Seventeenth century to 1837 in Nos. 26 and 27; 1832-1843 in the part of No. 28 read here, with the mail history reaching back to 1832 and the customs table starting at 1836
repository: Internet Archive, item fergushistorical2629unse (858 leaves), the Allen County Public Library copy. The deposit at chicago/reference/fergus/ holds the item's hOCR search text and hOCR page index; the 138 MB PDF named in that deposit's SOURCE.yaml is NOT in this repository. transcribes.work: No. 26 - William Henry Harrison, A Discourse on the Aborigines of the Ohio Valley, prepared at the request of the Historical Society of Ohio
transcribes.date: 1838 (the address); 1883 (this reprint). Describes prehistory and the seventeenth century.
transcribes.note: AN ARGUMENT, NOT A RECORD, and not about this town: Harrison contests Colden, Pownall, Franklin, Clinton and Haywood on the Iroquois conquest of the Ohio valley and never reaches the Illinois lakeshore. Swept in full; it yielded one claim, and that one only says what the number is.

transcribes.work: No. 26's appendix - speeches of Potawatomi and Miami chiefs at Fort Wayne, 2 October 1811, taken down at the time, with Hiram W. Beckwith's 1883 footnotes
transcribes.date: 1811 (the speeches); 1883 (the footnotes). Describes 1811, and the footnotes 1812.
transcribes.note: THE ONE PLACE IN NUMBER 26 THAT IS EVIDENCE. The speeches are contemporary minutes of an 1811 council and read at rung 2; Oseemit's is the earliest statement this project holds of what Chicago was to the people who lived there. Beckwith's FOOTNOTES to them are 1883 compilation at rung 4 and are cited as such, and two of them merely point at Mrs Kinzie's Wau-Bun, which this project already grades higher.

transcribes.work: No. 27 - Hiram W. Beckwith, The Illinois and Indiana Indians: the Potawatomi chapters, the village catalogue, the treaty list, and Henry R. Schoolcraft's eyewitness account of the Chicago treaty of August 1821, quoted at length from his own narrative journal
transcribes.date: 1884 (the printing). Describes the seventeenth century to 1837, and the Chicago material 1803-1834.
transcribes.note: THE PAYING PART OF THIS HALF, and it is two rungs in one chapter. Beckwith COMPILES at rung 3 - the village catalogue, the etymologies, the treaty count - out of treaties, government correspondence and his father's survey work; where he QUOTES Schoolcraft on the 1821 treaty he is transmitting an eyewitness journal, which is why the forest on the south branch, the level plain along the lake and the bower on the north bank are the strongest landscape claims in this file. Every claim says which of the two it is.

transcribes.work: No. 28 - Directory of the City of Chicago for 1843, compiled by Robert Fergus: read here through the title page, the introductory, and the civic pages to the port statistics (leaves 399-429)
transcribes.date: 1896 (the compilation and printing); the canvass beneath it is James W. Norris's of August to December 1843. Describes 1832-1843.
transcribes.note: A DIRECTORY FOR 1843 COMPILED IN 1896 BY A MAN WHO ARRIVED IN 1839, and it says so on its own title page and in its own preface. Everything in it descends from Norris's 1843 canvass, of which Fergus - who set its type - writes that 'sailors were made tailors, and tailors sailors, names were spelled at and locations guessed'. It is a fifty-three-year retrospective and nothing taken from it may be cited as a contemporary record. The same caution binds Fergus' Directory for 1839, published 1876, which is T-0506's subject.

what_it_supplies: the volume's own contents, which nothing in the project stated before: which four Fergus numbers are bound here, by whom, and at which leaves - written into data/research/books/README.md
the site of Chicago as an inhabited place before the plat: a scattered Potawatomi village on BOTH branches of the river, and the stream's name read as a skunk primarily and a wild onion secondarily
eyewitness landscape at the confluence in August 1821, through Schoolcraft: a belt of forest skirting the south branch, and beyond it the extensive level plain stretching to the lake shore

a temporary structure placed by two landmarks this project holds - an open seated bower on the green along the NORTH BANK, near the old John Kinzie house and directly under the guns of the fort - and with it a constraint on how built that bank can have been in 1821
the largest crowd figure the project holds for this ground: between two and three thousand assembled for the 1821 treaty, with provisions issued daily to about three thousand

the Chicago mail, year by year, across the scene date: horseback weekly in 1832 under Jonathan Nash Bailey, one-horse wagon under John S. C. Hogan, two-horse wagon in 1833, a SEMI-WEEKLY FOUR-HORSE STAGE FROM 1834 AND TRI-WEEKLY IN 1835, daily from 1837
an institution of the scene year's own town, dated to the day and not previously held here: the Chicago Lyceum, instituted 2 December 1834

the town eight years on, as a bound from above on 1835: seven churches placed to the block face, one of them measured (112 by 55 feet, walls 34 feet); St James' erected 1837 for about $10,000; a Masonic lodge in a THIRD STOREY at Clark and South Water; three military companies; a fire department under a chief engineer

the earliest customs figures for the port - 1836, exports $1,000.64 against imports $325,203.90 - and the custom house's own warning that both understate, because vessels arrived and departed unreported
a method statement for the 1843 city census: permanent residents only, transitory persons excluded in every instance

the provenance of the Chicago directories themselves, from the compiler of two of them: the 1839 directory is an 1876 publication, this one is 1896, and the 1843 canvass under both guessed at locations

any contemporary record of 1835. The two numbers that reach this town were printed in 1884 and 1896, about 1821 and about 1843 respectively, and NEITHER DESCRIBES THE SCENE YEAR AT ALL

any measured coordinate, lot or plat position. Every placement here is prose - 'along the north bank', 'between Washington and Madison' - and the 1843 addresses are in a street grid the compiler himself says was guessed at
the 1843 census figures. The OCR wove that table's six ward columns into lines of loose digits and this project will not transcribe a table it cannot read; bk_fer_057 records the refusal
page images, and therefore any scan_verified reading. The 138 MB PDF is not in the deposit and nobody here has seen a page
the second half of the volume - leaves 430-858, being the 1843 business directory and the whole of No. 29. That is T-0500, and this record will be extended by it rather than replaced

note: THE RECORD'S TIER IS 2 AND THAT IS THE 1811 SPEECHES' RUNG, NOT THE VOLUME'S. Three of the four pieces read here are compilation - Harrison arguing in 1838, Beckwith compiling in 1884, Fergus recollecting in 1896 - and every claim taken from them says so on its face and is cited at its own rung. The one piece that is evidence is the appendix to Number 26: minutes of a council at Fort Wayne on 2 October 1811, taken down at the time, which read at rung 2 and carry this record. A run reaching for 'Fergus on 1835' is reaching for a 1896 recension of an 1843 canvass and must cite it as that. THE ASK WAS FOR SETTLERS' REMINISCENCES AND THIS HALF OF THE VOLUME IS NOT THAT, which is the finding and not a failure of the reading. The Fergus numbers in general are where the settlers of the 1830s told their own stories; numbers 26 to 29 are a discourse on the mound-builders, a tribal history, a directory and a governor's life. The two that touch Chicago touch it either fourteen years too early (No. 27, and it is the better of the two: Schoolcraft walking onto the ground in 1821) or eight years too late (No. 28, and it is a retrospective at that). Twenty of the forty-one claims are town findings all the same, and they are recorded as bounds and corroborations rather than as placements: NOTHING IN data/structures/, data/assets/, data/residents/ OR data/households/ WAS CHANGED BY THIS READING.
